summary:
Zechariah son of Berechiah began prophesying in Jerusalem in the second year of Darius king of Persia (520 BC, 1:1). Babylon had burned the temple in 586 BC; returned exiles had begun rebuilding it, then stalled (Ezra 4:24). Ezra 5:1 names him alongside Haggai as the prophets who restarted the work, and the temple was finished in 516/515 BC (Ezra 6:15). Zechariah's name means "the LORD remembers," and the book opens with an offer: "Return to Me, declares the LORD of Hosts, and I will return to you" (1:3). "Hosts" means heaven's armies.

Chapters 1-6 record eight visions from a single night, decoded by an angel — the symbolic style later called apocalyptic, familiar from Daniel and Revelation. Horsemen patrol the earth among myrtle trees; four horns, the powers that scattered Judah, fall to four craftsmen; a surveyor measures Jerusalem, which God will guard as "a wall of fire" (2:5); Joshua the high priest (Israel's chief priest) is accused by Satan (Hebrew for "accuser") and given clean garments for filthy ones; a gold lampstand fed by two olive trees brings Zerubbabel, the governor rebuilding the temple, the word "Not by might nor by power, but by My Spirit" (4:6); a flying scroll carries a curse on thieves and perjurers; a woman named Wickedness is sealed in a basket and carried to Shinar (Babylonia); four chariots ride out to patrol the earth. The visions end in an act: Zechariah crowns Joshua and announces, "Here is a man whose name is the Branch" (6:11-12), a title Jeremiah 23:5 uses for a coming king from David's line; the Branch will build the temple of the LORD and sit as "a priest on His throne" (6:13).

Chapters 7-8 answer envoys who ask whether to keep the fast of the fifth month, the month the temple had burned (2 Kings 25:8-9). The reply repeats the earlier prophets' demand — "Administer true justice. Show loving devotion and compassion to one another" (7:9) — and promises that the mourning fasts will become "times of joy and gladness, cheerful feasts" (8:19), and that ten men from the nations will grasp one Jew's robe: "Let us go with you, for we have heard that God is with you" (8:23).

Chapters 9-14 are two oracles, each headed "the burden of the word of the LORD" (9:1; 12:1); "burden" translates the Hebrew massa, a weighty prophetic pronouncement. They carry no dates, never name the prophet, and look to a distant future; scholars differ over whether they come from Zechariah or a later hand, and much here is difficult, the shepherd story of chapter 11 especially. The Gospel accounts of Jesus' final week quote these chapters repeatedly. Zion's king arrives "righteous and victorious, humble and riding on a donkey" (9:9), quoted at the triumphal entry (Matthew 21:5; John 12:15). A rejected shepherd is paid thirty pieces of silver and told, "Throw it to the potter" (11:12-13), the scene Matthew applies to Judas's payment (Matthew 27:9-10, which credits the words to Jeremiah, often explained as a blended quotation). Jerusalem's people "will look on Me, the One they have pierced" (12:10), cited at the crucifixion (John 19:37). On the night of his arrest Jesus applies "Strike the Shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered" (13:7) to the disciples' coming desertion (Matthew 26:31; Mark 14:27).

The final chapter describes "a day of the LORD" (14:1): the nations gather against Jerusalem, the LORD goes out to fight, and the Mount of Olives splits in two (14:4). Living water flows from the city, and "the LORD will become King over all the earth" (14:9). The nations' survivors come yearly to keep the Feast of Tabernacles, Israel's autumn harvest festival (14:16; Leviticus 23:33-43). In the closing lines, "HOLY TO THE LORD" (the inscription on the high priest's gold turban plate, Exodus 28:36) appears on the bells of horses, and every cooking pot in Jerusalem and Judah is "holy to the LORD of Hosts" (14:20-21).
